cells.tense: You are looking at how a thing works instead of at the thing itself.
cells.ask: Let one pattern you've noticed sit unproven for a day, then hand it to someone with the reason you trust it.
cells.core:
You're standing somewhere the shape of things shows up with the labels off. The middle of an argument, the way a week goes, the order someone does a task in — you catch the shape before you can say where it came from, and the details aren't needed for you to trust it. People near you tend to feel steadier because something in the room makes sense.

The ordinary version of this is where you are. The turning-over is quick, it holds up, and it doesn't eat the day. Standing there, the next thing you're free to feed is structure that serves what it organizes — clear enough to lean on, the way a good frame holds a room. One pattern can sit unproven for a day before it goes anywhere.
cells.sheetLine: You catch the shape before you can say where it came from.

cells.place: a place where the shape of something shows with the labels peeled off

cells.tense: Somewhere ahead there is a puzzle you're racing to solve before anyone else needs it.
cells.ask: Say one insight out loud without dressing it up, then leave it there and see what they pick up.
cells.core:
You're turning things over harder than this moment calls for. A conversation gets picked apart for the shape under it, a silence gets a pattern assigned to it by next week. The explaining has taken the room the other person was standing in. What you spend on chasing it is the very thing you were after.

What settles this is not another pass. It's the charge of a direction you actually picked, ready to carry someone along, and that charge comes from something already grown to its end — not from one more round of proof. One insight, said plainly and left where it lands, is enough to start.

cells.tense: There was a door where a question landed badly, and you are still standing past it.
cells.ask: Ask one plain question about how something works, and let the answer change what you do next.
cells.core:
The watching is lean here. Not gone — lean. At some point the asking stopped paying, and you learned to take the surface and keep moving. So you act on what you're handed, quick and practical, and the shape underneath goes unread. It comes back around when something doesn't hold and there's no read to fall back on.

This isn't a thin supply of questions. It's a knower worn smooth. So don't push at the bare spot directly. Feed the charge that pulls it through: sit inside a situation you can't picture the end of, and stay long enough to wonder how it works. The watching fills back on its own once the wondering is welcome. One plain question, asked about a real thing.
cells.sheetLine: The watching isn't gone, it's just gone quiet.

cells.tense: The pattern is already in your hands while you talk as if someone else found it.
cells.ask: Name the one pattern you've already noticed and been calling a guess, out loud once.
cells.core:
You're already reading how things fit — the order under the task list, the shape of what someone isn't saying, the step everybody skips. It shapes what you do next, and it works. You just call it the data, or the setup, or what anyone would have seen. The reading is doing the labor and getting no name on it.

So bring the claim back to something simpler. What's right here is plain and shared: if the read is true, it can be owned out loud. You've already noticed this. You've been calling it a guess so it doesn't have to count. One pattern, named once without the hedge around it, is enough to start.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that this person's early attempts to question were punished; the record gives no history and Too Little may locate but not tell it, so I name the door and the sand without events. A reader could say they simply prefer to move instead of knowing, which is why the Too Much cell names the pressure to share an insight before it sits rather than the refusal to reflect. The ask survives a wrong read because catching one insight, saying nothing yet, then sharing it later with a reason is doable and teaches something either way. The sentence that serves me is 'you'd rather see what it does than ask why it does it' and it goes.
